title: Retrieval-of-Thought: Efficient Reasoning via Reusing Thoughts
claim: Sequential trial-and-error reasoning wastes tokens on wrong paths; retrieving and assembling a reusable template guides the model directly to the right path.
layout: 2 stacked panels, top baseline vs bottom method, left-to-right, divider line
description: A two-row diagram separated by a horizontal rule. The top row, titled Chain-of-Thought, shows a reasoning question going into an LRM box. The LRM output snakes through three rows of dashed-box nodes. Red nodes are labeled Wrong Path, and green nodes are labeled Right Path. Curved arrows connect the rows before the final green row reaches an orange Answer box. The bottom row, titled Retrieval-of-Thought, has a large dashed container with three stages joined by black arrows. These are a blue thought graph with an initial node, a reward-guided traversal that fades unselected nodes, and a retrieved template shown as a short blue chain. A blue arrow carries the template down to the LRM input. The LRM then produces a single green right path leading to Answer. A black curved arrow loops from the question back to the initial-node retrieval.
caption: The figure contrasts Chain-of-Thought (CoT) inference in LRMs with our Retrieval-of-Thought (RoT) approach. In CoT (top), models sequentially explore multiple wrong paths, causing inefficiency and high token usage. RoT (bottom) builds on a structured thought graph where reasoning steps are stored as nodes. First, RoT retrieves relevant nodes and performs reward-guided traversal to assemble a problem-specific template, reducing redundant exploration and directing the model toward correct reasoning. This yields more efficient inference and fewer tokens.
abstract: Large reasoning models improve accuracy by producing long reasoning traces, but this inflates latency and cost, motivating inference-time efficiency. We propose Retrieval-of-Thought (RoT), which reuses prior reasoning as composable ``thought" steps to guide new problems. RoT organizes steps into a thought graph with sequential and semantic edges to enable fast retrieval and flexible recombination. At inference, RoT retrieves query-relevant nodes and applies reward-guided traversal to assemble a problem-specific template that guides generation. This dynamic template reuse reduces redundant exploration and, therefore, reduces output tokens while preserving accuracy. We evaluate RoT on reasoning benchmarks with multiple models, measuring accuracy, token usage, latency, and memory overhead. Findings show small prompt growth but substantial efficiency gains, with RoT reducing output tokens by up to 40%, inference latency by 82%, and cost by 59% while maintaining accuracy. RoT establishes a scalable paradigm for efficient LRM reasoning via dynamic template construction through retrieval.
